newsitem.title: FINLAND: NATO row overshadows summit economic talks.
newsitem.headline: NATO row overshadows summit economic talks.

text.p: With the United States and Russia at loggerheads over NATO's expansion plans, a breakthrough on economic issues could provide a much-needed fillip for the Yeltsin-Clinton summit which starts on Thursday.
For the Americans, it would be a way of showing it was not out to isolate Russia and demonstrating support for a new, reform-oriented cabinet unveiled in Moscow this week.
For Russia, the NATO row is an opportunity to lean on Washington for concessions on the economic front, although officials repeatedly deny any link between the two.
But the Kremlin is also concerned not to appear beholden to Washington at a time when it is trying to rediscover some of the superpower muscle it lost with the collapse of communism.
This, plus the fact that some of Russia's demands involve not just the United States but other western powers, could get in the way of a major initiative.
Pre-summit negotiations have taken place firmly behind closed doors and few details have been released of even what is on the table.
Russia has, however, made it clear it feels it is time to join a string of international organisations and the United States has cautiously proffered an investment sweetner.

"What we are prepared to do as a government is to use institutions such as the Export-Import bank, OPIC the U.S. Russia Enterprise Fund, to make available financing that could support several billion dollars of investment," a senior U.S. official said on Friday in Washington.
But Russia has to improve the investment climate, he said.
The chaotic and frequently-changing regulations and corruption which have accompanied market reforms introduced in 1991 are leading concerns.

A spokesman for Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said the issue of Moscow's membership in various organisations came up in weekend talks with U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers.
The World Trade Organisation, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) and Paris Club of government creditors were on the list.
The two sides also discussed a bilateral document, he said, but gave no hint of what was in it.
Raf Sharikov, editor of Russia's biggest business newspaper Kommersant Daily, said the Americans were keen to stress the economic aspects of the summit.

"At a meeting with major Russian newspaper editors, Yeltsin referred to a telephone conversation with Clinton and said that the main discussion was that Clinton wanted the first issue to be an economic one and promised four billion dollars of investment in the Russian economy," he told Reuters.

"But Yeltsin clearly rejected that offer since he considered that that economic component would undermine the NATO negotiations. In that, if we get carte blanche here we should somehow give in on NATO expansion."
U.S. officials have concurred with Russia that the economy is number three on the summit agenda, after European security and bilateral arms control, although they have said it is an important issue.

They were not immediately available to comment on the comments by Sharikov, who said he was afraid any concessions on the economic front might fizzle out after July, when NATO is expected to invite in some of Moscow's former allies.
But Yastrzhembsky held out some hope when he said, without elaborating. "The summit consists of three big blocks of issues. A breakthrough is possible in one of them."
